blocks.text: Exod. XXIII, 1. Deut. XIX, 16. Ps. XXXV, 11. etc.

This very view has recently also found favour with Oedmann, who in vol. 3, Chapter 4, p. 45 ff. sought to prove that תחמס is strix Otus Linn. (die mittlere Ohreule, der kleine Schuhu). He relied above all on this argument: that خمش [khamasha] in the language of the Arabs means to wound with the claws, and that this fits very well that bird which, as Hasselquist reports (Travels p. 291), when in the evening it finds the windows open, enters houses and kills infants left without a guard. How flimsy this argument is, everyone will see for himself.

On the word תחמס, J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 825 ff. also deserves to be compared. To him too Bochart's opinion seems probable. But what chiefly prevents him from assenting is that it is contrary to Moses' custom to mention both sexes among the forbidden animals. Bochart himself has already met this doubt, both in this very passage and above, toward the end of the preceding Chapter.
